summary: Mint HTTP/1 response parser checks first Transfer-Encoding token instead of last, enabling response smuggling
description:
### Summary

Inconsistent Interpretation of HTTP Requests ('HTTP Request/Response Smuggling') vulnerability in elixir-mint mint allows a malicious HTTP/1 server to desynchronize an intermediary and the Mint client on a pooled connection, poisoning the responses to subsequent requests that share the connection.

`message_body/1` in `lib/mint/http1.ex` selects chunked framing when `chunked` is the first coding listed in a response's `Transfer-Encoding` fields. RFC 9112 section 6.3 applies chunked framing only when `chunked` is the final coding, and otherwise reads the body until the server closes the connection. For a response such as `Transfer-Encoding: chunked, gzip`, an intermediary that follows the RFC treats every byte up to the close as the body, while Mint ends the body at the zero-length chunk and parses the remaining bytes as the response to the next request on the connection.

Mint also keeps the connection open after an HTTP/1.0 response, final or 1xx, that carries `Transfer-Encoding` and `Connection: keep-alive`. RFC 9112 section 6.1 requires treating the framing of such a message as faulty and closing the connection after it, so bytes after its chunked body are parsed as the response to the next request in the same way.

### Details

**1. Coding list.** `store_header/3` in `lib/mint/http1.ex` tokenizes each `Transfer-Encoding` field with `Mint.HTTP1.Parse.transfer_encoding_header/1` and appends the codings to `request.transfer_encoding` in the order received.

**2. Framing decision.** `message_body/1` returns chunked framing when `List.first(request.transfer_encoding)` is `"chunked"`. The only other `Transfer-Encoding` check rejects a response that also carries `Content-Length`, so `chunked, gzip` on its own is framed as chunked.

**3. Leftover bytes.** `decode_body/5` ends the body at the zero-length chunk and its trailer section, and `next_request/3` keeps the rest of the data in `conn.buffer` or decodes it immediately as the next queued response. An RFC 9112 intermediary frames the same response as ending at connection close, so bytes it forwarded as body of the first response become the response to the next request on the Mint connection, and that request's real response is left in the buffer for the one after it.

**4. HTTP/1.0 keep-alive.** `request_done/2` keeps an HTTP/1.0 connection open when the response has `Connection: keep-alive`, without checking for `Transfer-Encoding`, and `decode_body(:informational, ...)` resets the framing state of a 1xx response and keeps parsing. An HTTP/1.0 response with `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` and `Connection: keep-alive` therefore leaves the connection open after its chunked body, and the following bytes are decoded as the next queued response, although RFC 9112 section 6.1 requires closing the connection after such a message.

### PoC

1. Start a loopback TCP server that answers the first request with `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` and `Transfer-Encoding: chunked, gzip`, the chunked body `5\r\nLEGIT\r\n0\r\n\r\n`, and directly after it the bytes `HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 8\r\n\r\nSMUGGLED`.
2. Connect with `Mint.HTTP1` and send a request. Mint returns `LEGIT` as the complete body, keeps the connection open, and holds the second response in `conn.buffer`.
3. Send a second request on the same connection and have the server answer it with a real response. Mint returns `SMUGGLED` as the response to the second request and keeps the real one in the buffer.
4. Pipelining both requests before the server answers gives the same result from a single `Mint.HTTP1.stream/2` call.

### Impact

A malicious or attacker-influenced HTTP/1 origin behind an intermediary that follows RFC 9112 framing can make the intermediary and the Mint client disagree on where a response ends. On a pooled keep-alive connection, bytes the origin appends to one response become the response to the next request sharing the connection, and the real responses shift to later requests.

### References

* Introducing commit: https://github.com/elixir-mint/mint/commit/60089586ec7adc9fddb09f69a2f5919ba9ac7f33

cwes.name: Inconsistent Interpretation of HTTP Requests ('HTTP Request/Response Smuggling')

summary: Mint HTTP/2 client buffers oversized frames to ~16 MiB before enforcing max_frame_size, enabling remote memory exhaustion
description:
## Summary

Mint's HTTP/2 client enforces its `max_frame_size` limit only after a complete frame payload has been received, not against the length field in the 9-byte frame header. Because the frame decoder pattern-matches on the full declared payload before the size guard can run, a malicious or compromised HTTP/2 server can announce a frame whose declared length is far larger than the client's advertised `max_frame_size` (default 16,384 bytes, header maximum 16,777,215 bytes) and then stream that payload slowly. The client accumulates every received byte in a per-connection buffer while the decoder repeatedly returns an incomplete-frame signal, so the buffer for a single connection can grow to roughly 16 MiB, about 1024 times the advertised limit, and can be pinned there indefinitely. Any Elixir or Erlang service that uses Mint as an HTTP/2 client against an untrusted or attacker-influenced origin is exposed with no application opt-in.

## Root Cause

The security invariant Mint intends to enforce is that no inbound frame exceeds the negotiated `max_frame_size`. That check is expressed as a guard on the decoded payload rather than on the declared length field, so it cannot fire until the whole payload is already buffered. The frame decoder uses an Erlang binary pattern match that requires the entire declared payload to be present as a contiguous binary before it succeeds; until then it returns an incomplete-frame result and the caller stores the growing binary. There is no comparison of the 24-bit header length field against `max_frame_size` before accumulation begins, and no independent cap on the connection buffer.

```elixir
# lib/mint/http2/frame.ex
def decode_next(bin, max_frame_size \\ 16_384) when is_binary(bin) do
  case decode_next_raw(bin) do
    {:ok, {_type, _flags, _stream_id, payload}, _rest}
    when byte_size(payload) > max_frame_size ->
      {:error, :payload_too_big}          # only reachable once the full payload is present
    {:ok, {type, flags, stream_id, payload}, rest} ->
      {:ok, decode_contents(type, flags, stream_id, payload), rest}
    :more ->
      :more
  end
end

defp decode_next_raw(<<
       length::24, type, flags, _reserved::1, stream_id::31,
       payload::size(length)-binary,        # requires all `length` bytes before matching
       rest::binary
     >>) do
  {:ok, {type, flags, stream_id, payload}, rest}
end

defp decode_next_raw(_other), do: :more   # returned for any partial frame
```

```elixir
# lib/mint/http2.ex
defp maybe_concat_and_handle_new_data(conn, data) do
  data = Util.maybe_concat(conn.buffer, data)   # unconditional concatenation, no size cap
  {conn, responses} = handle_new_data(conn, data, [])
  {:ok, conn, Enum.reverse(responses)}
end

defp handle_new_data(%__MODULE__{} = conn, data, responses) do
  case Frame.decode_next(data, conn.client_settings.max_frame_size) do
    :more ->
      conn = put_in(conn.buffer, data)          # stores the growing buffer with no size guard
      handle_consumed_all_frames(conn, responses)
    ...
  end
end
```

## Impact

The attacker must be, or must control, the HTTP/2 server that a Mint client connects to; no client-side authentication or non-default configuration is required. Once connected, the attacker can inflate the client's per-connection buffer to roughly 16 MiB and hold it there for as long as the connection stays open by withholding the final payload byte. The demonstrated capability is memory-resource exhaustion of the client process: with N connections to hostile origins the inflation is about 16 MiB times N, and transient peaks during binary concatenation can be roughly double the current buffer size. This is a remote, unauthenticated denial-of-service primitive against outbound HTTP/2 clients such as web-backend HTTP clients, webhook delivery systems, scrapers, federation and proxy components, and any client that follows redirects to third-party HTTP/2 origins. There is no bandwidth amplification: the attacker must transmit one byte for every byte the client buffers, which bounds the practical blast radius per connection but does not remove the 1024x gap between the advertised limit and actual enforcement.

## Proof of Concept

```text
The proof of concept exercises the frame decoder directly, which is the point at
which the size guard is bypassed. It shows that an oversized declared length
produces the incomplete-frame result during accumulation and only trips the size
error once the full payload is present, so the caller buffers everything in the
meantime. Requires an Elixir/OTP toolchain with the mint dependency available.
```

1. Build a 9-byte HTTP/2 frame header whose 24-bit length field declares 1,000,000 bytes, which exceeds the default `max_frame_size` of 16,384.
2. Feed the header plus incrementally larger partial payloads to the decoder and observe the incomplete-frame result each time.
3. Feed the complete declared payload and observe that the size error is only raised now, after the full payload has been buffered.

```elixir
max = 16_384
declared = 1_000_000
header = <<declared::24, 0, 0, 0::1, 1::31>>

# Partial payloads accumulate; guard never fires
:more = Mint.HTTP2.Frame.decode_next(header <> :binary.copy(<<0>>, 16_384), max)
:more = Mint.HTTP2.Frame.decode_next(header <> :binary.copy(<<0>>, 512_000), max)

# Only once the full declared payload is present does the guard trip
{:error, :payload_too_big} =
  Mint.HTTP2.Frame.decode_next(header <> :binary.copy(<<0>>, declared), max)
```

```text
:more
:more
{:error, :payload_too_big}
```

A server that streams `declared - 1` payload bytes and holds the connection open keeps the client in the accumulation state permanently, pinning the buffer at up to the declared size.

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** A Mint HTTP/2 client establishes an outbound connection to a server the attacker operates or controls, completing the connection preface and SETTINGS exchange with valid parameters. HTTP/2 client support ships in every release and requires no opt-in beyond using HTTP/2.
2. **Control:** The attacker fully controls the 9-byte frame header, including the 24-bit length field (up to 16,777,215), and the payload bytes streamed afterward. All of these values pass unmodified into the client's buffer and decoder.
3. **Path:** Inbound socket data reaches `stream/2` (or `recv/3`), which calls `maybe_concat_and_handle_new_data/2`. That unconditionally concatenates the new bytes onto `conn.buffer` via `Util.maybe_concat/2` and calls `handle_new_data/3`, which calls `Frame.decode_next/2`.
4. **Guard:** The `max_frame_size` guard in `Frame.decode_next/2` is expressed on the decoded payload, and `decode_next_raw/1` requires the entire declared payload before its binary pattern match succeeds. For any partial oversized frame the decoder returns the incomplete-frame result, so the guard is structurally unreachable during accumulation. No independent buffer cap exists.
5. **Primitive:** On the incomplete-frame result, `handle_new_data/3` stores the full accumulated binary back into `conn.buffer` with no size check, and the cycle repeats on subsequent socket data.
6. **Result:** The single-connection buffer grows to roughly the declared frame length, up to about 16 MiB, roughly 1024 times the advertised `max_frame_size`, and stays there while the connection is held open, exhausting client process memory across enough connections.

## Bypass Evidence

The only size control on the affected path is the `max_frame_size` guard in `Frame.decode_next/2`. It does not block this path because `decode_next_raw/1`'s binary pattern match, `payload::size(length)-binary`, is atomic in the Erlang virtual machine: it either matches with the complete declared payload present or fails entirely and returns the incomplete-frame result. There is no intermediate state in which the header is parsed but the payload is not, so the guard cannot run until the payload is fully buffered. Nine disproof attempts were made and all failed to prevent accumulation: TCP and inet receive buffers only bound individual socket deliveries, not the cumulative connection buffer; HTTP/2 flow control applies only to DATA frames, is evaluated after a frame is decoded, is not enforced for receive-window violations in this client, and the default connection window already equals the maximum frame length; Mint has no connection idle timeout that releases the buffer; the consumed-frames handler checks only GOAWAY state; CONTINUATION header-list limits apply to a separate structure; active and passive socket modes converge on the same accumulation function; SETTINGS validation constrains parameter ranges, not subsequent frame sizes; and the buffer accumulation function performs no size check. This weakness is distinct from the previously published advisory CVE-2026-48862 (GHSA-g586-ccqf-7x4r), which concerns unbounded growth of the per-connection stream map via PUSH_PROMISE frames; that fix, released in 1.9.0, modified only the connection module and its tests and did not touch the frame decoder or the connection buffer, so it does not cover or block this path.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: erlang (Hex.pm)`
- `Package: mint`
- `Affected range: >= 0.1.0, < 1.11.0`
- `Fixed in: 1.11.0`

The incomplete-frame accumulation path was added with the HTTP/2 connection in commit 596ca43, first released in 0.1.0, and is unchanged through 1.10.1. Version 1.11.0 checks the declared length in the frame header against `max_frame_size` before buffering the payload.

## Suggested Fix

Enforce `max_frame_size` against the declared length field in the 9-byte frame header before buffering or decoding the payload. A minimal approach is to inspect the leading 24-bit length in `Frame.decode_next/2` and return the too-big error immediately when it exceeds `max_frame_size`, so oversized frames are rejected from the header alone and the connection buffer can never exceed roughly `max_frame_size` plus the header size. The remediation must cover every caller that feeds inbound bytes into the decoder, including both active-mode `stream/2` and passive-mode `recv/3`, since both share the same accumulation path. As an interim mitigation without a code change, operators can avoid initiating HTTP/2 connections to untrusted or attacker-influenced origins and can bound the memory of processes that hold Mint connections; there is no configuration setting that moves the enforcement point earlier.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

cwes.name: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

summary: HPACK-indexed cookie fields in Mint HTTP/2 responses bypass max_header_list_size and exhaust client memory
description:
### Summary

Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in elixir-mint mint allows a malicious HTTP/2 server to exhaust memory on the client host and cause a denial of service.

`Mint.HTTP2` enforces the client's `max_header_list_size` setting only on the compressed size of an inbound header block, while RFC 9113 section 6.5.2 defines the limit on the decoded header list. An HPACK indexed field costs one byte on the wire and decodes to a dynamic table entry of up to 4 KB, and `join_cookie_headers/1` in `lib/mint/http2.ex` copies every `cookie` value of a response into one new binary. A header block under the default 256 KB wire limit therefore makes the client allocate about 1 GB for a single response, and several such responses in one delivery exhaust the memory of the process that owns the connection or of the whole VM.

### Details

**1. Compressed-size check only.** `Mint.HTTP2.assert_header_block_within_max_size/2` compares the accumulated `HEADERS` plus `CONTINUATION` bytes with `client_settings.max_header_list_size`, which bounds a `CONTINUATION` chain but not the decoded size. After `HPAX.decode/2` returns, `decode_hbf_and_add_responses/5` passes the header list to `handle_decoded_headers_for_stream/5` without measuring it. The only implementation of the RFC 9113 section 6.5.2 formula, `assert_headers_smaller_than_max_header_list_size/2`, applies the server's setting to headers Mint sends.

**2. Indexed-field expansion.** An HPACK indexed field (RFC 7541 section 6.1) is one byte for small table indexes and refers to a dynamic table entry of up to 4 KB. HPAX returns one shared binary per reference, so the decoded list itself stays small.

**3. Cookie join.** `join_cookie_headers/1` runs `Enum.map_join/3` over every `cookie` value, copying each shared value into one contiguous binary. The dynamic table entry persists for the connection, so the same block can answer every open stream, and `Mint.HTTP.stream/2` returns all responses parsed from one delivery together.

### PoC

1. Connect a `Mint.HTTP2` client with default `client_settings` to a server that writes raw HTTP/2 frames, and open a request.
2. Answer with a header block that stores one large `cookie` value in the HPACK dynamic table and then references it many times with indexed fields, keeping the compressed block under the 262,144-byte limit.
3. Mint accepts the block and returns one `cookie` header thousands of times larger than the wire bytes; the reporter measured a 1,047,808,858-byte value from 262,296 wire bytes on mint 1.10.1.
4. Answering several open requests in one delivery adds up: four responses held 4,240,710,592 bytes of cookie values at once.
5. A block of 60,000 references costs about 240 MB under the `cookie` field name and about 5 MB under a non-cookie name, which isolates `join_cookie_headers/1` as the amplifier.

### Impact

A malicious or compromised HTTP/2 server can make a Mint client allocate about 1 GB per response with default settings, exhausting host memory until the operating system kills the BEAM. HTTP/2 connection pools in Finch and Req, webhook and scraper clients, and reverse proxies fetching from untrusted upstreams are affected without any opt-in.

### Workarounds

Lower `client_settings: [max_header_list_size: n]` in `Mint.HTTP.connect/4`. The compressed check still applies, and each byte of the block can expand to at most one 4 KB table entry, so a limit of 4,096 bounds a response to roughly 16 MB. Alternatively, restrict connections to untrusted servers to HTTP/1 with `protocols: [:http1]`, which avoids the HTTP/2 receive path entirely. Do not set `max_header_list_size: :infinity`, which disables the compressed check as well.

### References

* Introducing commit: https://github.com/elixir-mint/mint/commit/8e0e04680476f90f9f68db4dfeabcbe66dabfc4d

summary: HTTP/1 chunk-size line tail is not validated in Mint, enabling response-framing desync
description:
### Summary

Mint's HTTP/1 chunked-body decoder validates only the hexadecimal digits of a chunk-size line and skips every byte between the last digit and the CRLF. RFC 9112 permits only a `;`-introduced chunk extension there. On a pooled keep-alive connection that traverses an RFC-strict intermediary, a malicious origin can send chunk-size lines that Mint accepts but the intermediary rejects, producing a response-smuggling primitive against subsequent requests on the connection.

### Details

`Mint.HTTP1.Parse.chunk_size/1` in `lib/mint/http1/parse.ex` stops at the first non-hexadecimal byte and returns the remainder unexamined. `Mint.HTTP1.decode_body/5` in `lib/mint/http1.ex` then hands that remainder to `Parse.ignore_until_crlf/1`, which advances over any byte until it finds CRLF. The accepted grammar is therefore `1*HEXDIG *OCTET CRLF`:

- `5ZZZZZ`, `5 anything at all`, `5<TAB>foo`, `5 9` and `5}~!` are accepted as chunk size 5.
- `0ZZZZ` and `0 9` are accepted as the terminating zero-length chunk and end the body.
- `5;name=value`, a legal chunk extension, is accepted and must stay accepted.

The sibling `Content-Length` parser, `Mint.HTTP1.Parse.content_length_header/1`, trims trailing whitespace and requires the whole remaining value to be digits, so the two parsers disagree about the same class of input.

The fix adds `Mint.HTTP1.Parse.chunk_extensions/1`, which accepts only optional whitespace, `;`-introduced extensions with token or quoted-string values, and the CRLF, and returns `:invalid_chunk_size` for anything else on both data chunks and the terminating chunk.

### PoC

1. Serve one `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` response with `transfer-encoding: chunked` from a loopback TCP server that controls the chunk-size line exactly.
2. Connect with `Mint.HTTP1` (mint 1.10.0) and stream the response.
3. Chunk-size lines `+5`, `Z5` and `00000000000000005` are refused with `:invalid_chunk_size`, confirming the earlier chunk-size fixes are present.
4. `5ZZZZZ`, `5 anything at all`, `5<TAB>foo`, `5 9` and `5}~!` are each accepted with body `hello`; `0ZZZZ` and `0 9` in place of the final `0` are accepted and end the body.
5. `Content-Length: +5`, `5ZZZ` and `5 9` are refused with `:invalid_content_length_header` in the same run.

### Impact

An attacker who controls or influences an HTTP/1 origin that a Mint client talks to through an RFC-strict pooled intermediary can make the intermediary and Mint disagree on chunk boundaries and on where the response ends, so bytes from one response are attributed to the next request sharing the connection. No smuggling chain against a specific intermediary was built; the divergence requires a fronting element stricter than Mint.

### References

- Introduction commit: 6008958
- Patch commit: c823778

cwes.name: Inconsistent Interpretation of HTTP Requests ('HTTP Request/Response Smuggling')

summary: Quadratic chunk-size parsing in Mint.HTTP1 allow a malicious server to exhaust client memory/CPU and crash the calling process
description:
### Summary

Mint's HTTP/1 parser reads a chunked response's chunk-size field with an algorithm whose cost grows quadratically in the number of digits, and it caps neither the digit count nor the work. A malicious or attacker-influenced server can send a chunk size made of a huge run of hex digits and burn CPU on the client host, causing a denial of service.

### Details

Each chunk in a chunked response is preceded by its size in hexadecimal. Mint reads that field digit by digit into an arbitrary-precision accumulator with no digit limit, so as the field grows the per-digit multiplication stops being constant time and one pass over N digits costs on the order of N squared. Because Mint re-parses from the start of its buffer on every socket message, dribbling the digits out in small packets makes the client repeat that growing cost.

### PoC

1. Run a server that sends a valid response head with `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, then, where the chunk size belongs, streams a long run of hex digits (for example the character `f`) instead of a real size followed by a CRLF.
2. Have the target application make any request that resolves to this server, for example via an attacker-controlled URL or a redirect to one.
3. Send the digits in small packets and keep the connection open. Each packet forces a full re-parse, and CPU on the client climbs sharply as the digit count grows.

### Impact

A remote server can consume large amounts of client CPU with a single chunked response, stalling the process that owns the connection and denying service to legitimate work. Any application that fetches attacker-influenceable URLs is exposed, such as webhooks, link unfurlers, URL previews, and metadata fetchers.

### References

* Introducing commit: https://github.com/elixir-mint/mint/commit/fc7d16538db7e40b56ed489f08683225cb0197fa
* Patch commit: https://github.com/elixir-mint/mint/commit/bd2a4e7513594997c140cfef9fe0e968712fb588

summary: Unbounded response-line buffering in Mint.HTTP1 allow a malicious server to exhaust client memory/CPU and crash the calling process
description:
### Summary

Mint's HTTP/1 response parser bounds the header section (`:max_header_list_size`, v1.9.2 / CVE-2026-58229) and the chunk body (v1.9.1 / CVE-2026-56810). Three parser states sit outside both budgets and are unbounded: the **status line**, the **chunk-extension** line, and the **chunk-size digits**.

A server that never sends a CRLF makes Mint buffer its output without limit. The chunk-size case additionally folds every hex digit into an arbitrary-precision accumulator with no digit cap, making one parse O(N²), and Mint re-parses the whole buffer on every socket message. Past the BEAM's bignum ceiling, `acc * 16` raises `SystemLimitError`, which escapes the public API as an **exception** instead of the documented `{:error, conn, reason, responses}` tuple.

Stock defaults throughout; `:max_header_list_size` was at 256 KiB and correctly enforced during every measurement below.

### Details

**1. Status line**: `lib/mint/http1.ex:722` (v1.9.3) / `:730` (`main`):

```elixir
:more ->
  conn = put_in(conn.buffer, data)
  {:ok, conn, responses}
```

`check_header_section_size/2` is only called from `decode_headers/5` and `decode_trailer_headers/4`. The status line is parsed before either, so the cap never applies.

**2. Chunk extension**: `lib/mint/http1.ex:869-879` (v1.9.3) / `:892-902` (`main`). `decode_body({:chunked, :metadata, size}, ...)` delegates to `Parse.ignore_until_crlf/1` and stores the buffer uncapped on `:more`. Same defect, reached through a response whose status line and headers are entirely valid.

**3. Chunk size**: `lib/mint/http1/parse.ex:26-37`:

```elixir
defp parse_hex_prefix(<<char, rest::binary>>, acc) when is_hex_digit(char) do
  parse_hex_prefix(rest, acc * 16 + hex_digit_value(char))   # no digit limit
end
```

`N` hex digits build a `4N`-bit bignum, so `acc * 16` is not constant time and one pass is O(N²). `handle_data/2` prepends `conn.buffer` and re-parses from the start on every socket message, so the attacker controls how many times that cost is paid via packet size.
Single-pass cost of `:binary.copy("f", n)`: 64 KiB → 0.23 s, 256 KiB → 2.96 s,
512 KiB → 11.3 s, 1000 KiB → 43.0 s.

The bignum ceiling on OTP 29.0.5 / erts 17.0.5 is 4,194,235 bits = **1,048,558 hex digits**
(~1 MiB of `f`). Beyond it:

```
RAISED SystemLimitError: a system limit has been reached
    (erts 17.0.5) :erlang.*(<bignum>, 16)
    (mint 1.9.3) lib/mint/http1/parse.ex:33: Mint.HTTP1.Parse.parse_hex_prefix/2
    (mint 1.9.3) lib/mint/http1.ex:850:      Mint.HTTP1.decode_body/5
    (mint 1.9.3) lib/mint/http1.ex:532:      Mint.HTTP1.handle_data/2
```

**Scope:** `Mint.HTTP1.Parse` is `@moduledoc false`, but no internal API call is required.
Every result below came from `Mint.HTTP.connect/4` plus the public `Mint.HTTP.stream/2`, against stock `mint 1.9.3` from Hex with default options.

### PoC

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# Minimal PoC server for all three unbounded parser states in Mint.HTTP1 <= 1.9.3.
# Usage: python3 evil_server_min.py [status|chunkext|chunksize]
# Then point any Mint/Finch/Req/Tesla client at http://127.0.0.1:8099/
import socket, sys

MODES = {
    # never send the CRLF that ends the status line
    "status": (b"HTTP/1.1 200 ", b"A" * 4096),
    # valid headers; never end the chunk-extension line
    "chunkext": (b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nTransfer-Encoding: chunked\r\n\r\n5;", b"A" * 4096),
    # valid headers; unbounded run of hex digits where the chunk size goes.
    # smaller packets are worse for the victim: each one triggers a full re-parse
    "chunksize": (b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nTransfer-Encoding: chunked\r\n\r\n", b"f" * 4096),
}
head, flood = MODES[sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "chunksize"]

srv = socket.socket()
srv.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
srv.bind(("127.0.0.1", 8099))
srv.listen(1)
conn, _ = srv.accept()
conn.recv(65536)
conn.sendall(head)

sent = 0
try:
    while True:
        conn.sendall(flood)
        sent += len(flood)
except (BrokenPipeError, ConnectionResetError):
    print(f"client died after {sent:,} bytes")
```

Against stock `mint 1.9.3`, driving it through `Mint.HTTP.stream/2`:

```
status    : UNBOUNDED BUFFER 95 MB, cap=262144   (163 ms)
chunkext  : UNBOUNDED BUFFER 96 MB, cap=262144   (11689 ms)
chunksize : RAISED SystemLimitError out of Mint.HTTP.stream/2   (64108 ms)
```

Left running, the status-line case reaches **1 GB buffered on one connection in 10.8 s**
(BEAM total 1.12 GB). Elixir PoCs and a 1 GB OOM demo available on request.

### Impact

Any application fetching a URL an attacker can influence — webhooks, link unfurling, URL previews, SSRF-adjacent fetchers, OIDC/JWKS metadata, scrapers, etc. Mint is the transport under Finch and therefore Req, Tesla and Swoosh.

1. **Uncaught exception:** `Mint.HTTP.stream/2` is specced as `{:ok, ...} | {:error, ...} | :unknown` and raises instead, so a caller that correctly handles the documented error tuple is still killed. Mint is process-less, so the crash lands in whichever process owns the connection (a pool worker, under Finch). Cost to the attacker: **~1 MB of one repeated character**, sent in 0.0 s, after which they can disconnect while the victim spends ~70 s dying.
2. **Unbounded memory:** 1 GB on a single connection in 10.8 s. Nothing crashes on the way, so no supervisor intervenes; the endpoint is the OOM killer taking out the whole `beam.smp` process.
3. **Bypasses header inspection:** In case 2 the status line and headers are valid, so a proxy or WAF sees a normal 200, and the v1.9.1 chunk-body fix does not apply because the parser never reaches a body.

These are three instances of one defect: `check_header_section_size/2` is wired into two of the five parser states that accept unbounded input. **Fixing only one leaves the others exploitable with a one line change to the attacker's server.**

### Proposed fix

Two changes. First, reuse the existing `:max_header_list_size` budget at the three unbounded `:more` sites:

```elixir
defp check_response_line_size(%{max_header_list_size: :infinity}, _size), do: :ok

defp check_response_line_size(%{max_header_list_size: max_size}, size)
     when size <= max_size,
     do: :ok

defp check_response_line_size(%{max_header_list_size: max_size}, size),
  do: {:error, {:response_line_too_long, size, max_size}}
```

Second, bound the digit count so the accumulator stays fixed-width, which removes both the quadratic behaviour and the `SystemLimitError`:

```elixir
@max_chunk_size_digits 32   # 128 bits, far beyond any real chunk

defp parse_hex_prefix(_binary, _acc, digits) when digits >= @max_chunk_size_digits do
  :error
end

defp parse_hex_prefix(<<char, rest::binary>>, acc, digits) when is_hex_digit(char) do
  parse_hex_prefix(rest, acc * 16 + hex_digit_value(char), digits + 1)
end
```

All three attacks then fail closed in 0-3 ms with documented error tuples
(`{:response_line_too_long, 524301, 262144}`, `:invalid_chunk_size`).

### Workarounds

None via configuration; `:max_header_list_size` does not cover these paths. Until a fix ships: restrict outbound HTTP/1 to trusted hosts, or run connections in a process with `Process.flag(:max_heap_size, ...)` to contain the allocation and isolate the exception.

summary: HTTP/1 chunk-size desync in Mint via Integer.parse/2 sign tolerance
description:
### Summary

Mint's HTTP/1 chunked-body decoder parses `chunk-size` lines with `Integer.parse(data, 16)`, which accepts a leading `+` or `-` in violation of RFC 7230. On a pooled keep-alive connection that traverses an RFC-strict intermediary, a malicious origin can send sign-prefixed chunk sizes that Mint accepts but the intermediary rejects, producing a response-smuggling primitive against subsequent requests on the connection.

### Details

`Mint.HTTP1.decode_body/5` in `lib/mint/http1.ex` dispatches on `Integer.parse(data, 16)` when reading the next chunk-size line. Because `Integer.parse/2` treats a leading `+`/`-` as an optional sign:

- `+5` is accepted as a five-byte chunk.
- `+0` and `-0` are accepted as the terminating zero-length chunk and end the body early.
- Only `-5` and other negative non-zero values fall through to `:invalid_chunk_size`.

A strict RFC 7230 parser rejects any sign in `chunk-size`, so Mint and an intermediary in the response path disagree on chunk boundaries. On a pooled keep-alive connection the origin can emit trailing bytes that the intermediary treats as body but Mint reads as the next response, poisoning the response queue for other in-flight requests on the shared socket.

The fix introduces `Mint.HTTP1.Parse.chunk_size/1` in `lib/mint/http1/parse.ex`, a strict `HEXDIG`-only parser that rejects any sign or non-hex prefix, and switches `decode_body/5` to use it.

### PoC

1. Point a Mint HTTP/1 client at an attacker-controlled origin through a strict HTTP/1 intermediary that reuses keep-alive connections.
2. Have the origin respond with `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` and a first chunk-size line of `+0\r\n\r\n`, followed by a crafted second "response" starting with `HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n...`.
3. The intermediary rejects `+0` and keeps reading; Mint treats `+0` as the last chunk and parses the crafted bytes as the next response on the pooled connection.

### Impact

An attacker who controls or influences an HTTP/1 origin that a Mint client talks to through an RFC-strict pooled intermediary can inject responses that Mint attributes to unrelated in-flight requests, corrupting response bodies, headers, or status codes seen by the application.

### References

* Introduction commit: https://github.com/elixir-mint/mint/commit/60089586ec7adc9fddb09f69a2f5919ba9ac7f33
* Patch commit: https://github.com/elixir-mint/mint/commit/fc7d16538db7e40b56ed489f08683225cb0197fa

summary: Incomplete CONTINUATION-flood fix: zero-length HTTP/2 CONTINUATION frames bypass the byte-size cap
description:
### Summary

Mint's HTTP/2 CONTINUATION-frame handler bounds the header-block accumulator only by total byte size. A remote HTTP/2 server reachable by the Mint client (directly, via SSRF, via an attacker-controlled redirect target, or via a man-in-the-middle) can open a stream with a `HEADERS` frame that omits `END_HEADERS` and then stream zero-length `CONTINUATION` frames indefinitely; because each frame adds zero bytes it never trips the size cap, yet each one still nests the accumulator on the connection, growing client memory in proportion to the frame count.

### Details

`Mint.HTTP2.handle_continuation/3` in `lib/mint/http2.ex` appends the header-block fragment carried by every incoming `CONTINUATION` frame to `conn.headers_being_processed`, which stores `{stream_id, iodata_acc, callback, byte_size_so_far}`. The accumulator is only consumed and cleared once a frame with the `END_HEADERS` flag arrives.

The only guard is `Mint.HTTP2.assert_header_block_within_max_size/2`, which checks the running byte total against the locally advertised `SETTINGS_MAX_HEADER_LIST_SIZE` (default 256 KB). The check trips only when `acc_size + byte_size(hbf_chunk)` exceeds the limit, so a fragment with `byte_size == 0` cannot trigger it. There is no independent cap on the number of `CONTINUATION` frames per header block, and the HTTP/2 frame decoder in `lib/mint/http2/frame.ex` accepts empty payloads as protocol-valid.

The result is that a peer that never emits `END_HEADERS` and only sends zero-length `CONTINUATION` frames keeps the accumulator open forever. Every frame adds roughly one cons cell (~16 bytes retained) for a 9-byte frame header on the wire, giving weak but nonzero amplification; sustained bandwidth from the peer is enough to grow the BEAM node's resident set until the operating system out-of-memory-kills it.

### PoC

1. Point a Mint HTTP/2 client at an attacker-controlled origin (direct connection, SSRF, or an auto-followed redirect).
2. From that origin, respond to any stream with a `HEADERS` frame that does not set `END_HEADERS`.
3. Follow up with a continuous stream of `CONTINUATION` frames on the same stream, each with a zero-length payload and without `END_HEADERS`; never emit the terminating frame.
4. `conn.headers_being_processed` on the client grows by one nesting per frame; sustained delivery drives the BEAM node to memory exhaustion.

### Impact

Any application using Mint as an HTTP/2 client is exposed when it can be induced to talk to an attacker-controlled server, whether directly, through an auto-followed redirect, through SSRF, or through a network man-in-the-middle. The consequence is progressive memory growth on the client node, ending in an out-of-memory termination of the entire Mint-using process.

### References

* Introduction commit: https://github.com/elixir-mint/mint/commit/596ca4304504be68939c4929e0831557097962b8
* Patch commit: https://github.com/elixir-mint/mint/commit/5779de1666344b32aefc4354184ea07f902f73ce

summary: Unbounded HTTP/1 response-header and chunked-trailer accumulation allows memory-exhaustion DoS
description:
### Summary

Mint's HTTP/1 response parser accumulates every parsed response header (and every chunked-trailer header) into an unbounded per-request list that only clears when the terminating blank line arrives. A remote HTTP server reachable by the Mint client (directly, via SSRF, via an attacker-controlled redirect target, or via a man-in-the-middle) can stream complete header or trailer lines forever, growing connection state on the client until the BEAM node is killed by the operating system's out-of-memory handler.

### Details

**1. Unbounded response-header accumulator.** `Mint.HTTP1.decode_headers/5` in `lib/mint/http1.ex` walks the response header section by calling the underlying line parser and prepending each `{name, value}` tuple to a growing list. When the incoming TCP segment ends mid-section, the accumulated list is stashed in `request.headers_buffer` and the trailing bytes in `conn.buffer`, ready to resume on the next `Mint.HTTP1.stream/2` invocation. The section is only released when the parser returns `:eof` (the terminating blank line), and nothing in between caps the number of headers or the byte size of the section.

**2. Same pattern for chunked trailers.** `Mint.HTTP1.decode_trailer_headers/4` reuses the same accumulator-plus-`headers_buffer` shape for HTTP/1.1 chunked trailers. After a zero-size chunk, the parser enters trailer mode and every trailer line is prepended to a list stored on the request across `stream/2` calls, again only terminated by `:eof`.

**3. Underlying parser has no built-in cap.** `Mint.HTTP1.Response.decode_header/1` in `lib/mint/http1/response.ex` invokes `:erlang.decode_packet(:httph_bin, binary, [])` with an empty option list, so the `packet_size` and `line_length` options both default to 0 (unlimited). No layer between the socket and the accumulator constrains the section.

**4. Denial of service.** A malicious server sends the status line (or, for the trailer variant, `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` plus a small chunk followed by `0\r\n`) and then streams complete header or trailer lines indefinitely without ever writing the closing blank line. The client's `conn` state grows on every `stream/2` call, driving the BEAM process resident set until the OS OOM-kills the node.

### PoC

1. Point a Mint HTTP/1 client at an attacker-controlled origin (direct connection, SSRF, or a redirect the client auto-follows).
2. From that origin, respond with `HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n` followed by a stream of minimal header lines (`A:\r\n`, or larger `X-Pad-N: <junk>\r\n` for faster growth) and never emit the closing `\r\n`.
3. The client's normal `Mint.HTTP1.stream/2` receive loop grows `request.headers_buffer` and `conn.buffer` on every packet until the BEAM node is OOM-killed. The chunked-trailer variant substitutes `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, a single small chunk, `0\r\n`, and then an endless stream of trailer lines.

### Impact

Any application using Mint as an HTTP/1 client is vulnerable whenever it can be induced to talk to an attacker-controlled server, whether directly, through an auto-followed redirect, through SSRF, or through a network man-in-the-middle. A single such connection is enough to exhaust the BEAM node's memory and terminate the entire application process.

### References

* Introduction commit: https://github.com/elixir-mint/mint/commit/3e6de4bac4821b0eb4d6109e8b1f3fb6458792c8
* Patch commit: https://github.com/elixir-mint/mint/commit/566d702e6f29105f77522ca7aabb9f64f2f4e333

summary: Chunked response decoder buffers an entire chunk in memory before emitting it
description:
### Summary

Mint (`Mint.HTTP1`) contains an unbounded-memory denial of service in its chunked transfer-encoding decoder. When decoding a `chunked` response body, Mint buffers every partial fragment of the current chunk in memory and does not release it to the caller until the full declared chunk length has arrived. The chunk size is read straight from the server and parsed with no upper bound, so a malicious or compromised server can announce one enormous chunk and then dribble bytes without ever completing it, forcing the client to accumulate the whole (never-finished) chunk in memory. Any unauthenticated remote server that a Mint client can be steered to reach (via a redirect, SSRF, or webhook fetch) can trigger it.

### Details

The bug lives in `Mint.HTTP1`'s chunked-body decoder in `lib/mint/http1.ex`, primarily `decode_body/5` and its helper `add_body_to_buffer/2`.

**1. Unbounded chunk-size parsing.** The chunk size line is parsed with `Integer.parse(data, 16)` with no maximum. A server can declare a chunk of arbitrary size, e.g. a size line of `7FFFFFFF` (~2 GiB).

**2. Buffer-until-complete decoding.** For a chunk of declared `size`, the decoder computes `new_size = size - byte_size(data)` and, while the chunk is not yet complete (`new_size > 0`), appends every received fragment to `request.data_buffer` via `add_body_to_buffer/2` (an unbounded iolist). Data is only emitted to the caller once the full declared length has been received, when `add_body/3` collapses and flushes the accumulated buffer. Because the chunk never completes, the buffer grows without bound and no `{:data, ...}` responses are ever produced.

**3. Streaming contract bypass.** This is worse than a plain large-body issue. The `content-length` path emits each received packet immediately via `add_body/3`, so a caller that safely streams large `content-length` bodies still gets forced to buffer the entire chunk in the `chunked` case. The caller cannot observe or bound the growth because no data responses are emitted at all until the chunk finishes.

The same "no size limit on server-controlled data" root cause also affects the unbounded header count in `decode_headers/5` and the unbounded chunk-size line buffer, but the chunked-body path is the most concrete because it bypasses streaming entirely.

### PoC

1. Stand up an attacker-controlled TCP server that accepts a Mint connection and replies with `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`, `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, then a chunk size line of `7FFFFFFF\r\n` (~2 GiB).
2. Dribble body bytes (e.g. 64 KiB packets) continuously without ever sending the chunk terminator, and hold the connection open.
3. Point a normal Mint client at the server (`Mint.HTTP.connect` + `Mint.HTTP.request`) and drain the socket via `Mint.HTTP.recv`.
4. Observe that zero `{:data, ...}` responses are emitted to the caller while process memory grows in lockstep with the dribbled bytes (measured ~506 MiB buffered for 500 MiB dribbled), climbing until out-of-memory.

### Impact

A remote attacker who controls or has compromised a server that a Mint client connects to can drive the client's memory arbitrarily high and trigger an out-of-memory condition, crashing the application. No client-side authentication is required, and applications that follow redirects, fetch user-supplied URLs (SSRF), or process webhooks are the most exposed; callers that otherwise stream large bodies safely gain no protection.

### References

* Introduction commit: https://github.com/elixir-mint/mint/commit/c575d819d39ebf7e9b77ec24584a5ffbb11c844e
* Patch commit: https://github.com/elixir-mint/mint/commit/193ce714907d16e8adc4ab3c40e4f0c2f045b2a6

summary: Unbounded streams map growth via PUSH_PROMISE without follow-up HEADERS
description:
### Summary

Mint's HTTP/2 client accepts `PUSH_PROMISE` frames from any server it connects to and inserts every promised stream into a per-connection map without consulting `max_concurrent_streams`. A malicious or compromised HTTP/2 server can flood the client with `PUSH_PROMISE` frames and withhold the matching response `HEADERS`, pinning one map entry per frame indefinitely until the client process runs out of memory.

### Details

`'Elixir.Mint.HTTP2':handle_push_promise/3` in `lib/mint/http2.ex` dispatches every inbound `PUSH_PROMISE` frame to `'Elixir.Mint.HTTP2':decode_push_promise_headers_and_add_response/5`, which inserts a `:reserved_remote` entry into `conn.streams` for the promised ID. The only validation applied is that the promised ID is even and not already present; `client_settings.max_concurrent_streams` is not consulted at promise time.

The concurrency cap is only checked when the response `HEADERS` for the promised stream arrive. A server that emits `PUSH_PROMISE` frames and never sends the matching `HEADERS` never trips that check, and the existing tally counts only streams in open states, not `:reserved_remote` entries.

HTTP/2 server push is accepted by default (`client_settings.enable_push` defaults to `true`), so no application opt-in is required. A single long-lived HTTP/2 connection to a hostile server lets it pin one `conn.streams` entry per `PUSH_PROMISE` frame, with no upper bound.

### PoC

1. Stand up a raw TCP HTTP/2 server that completes the handshake and ACKs the client's `SETTINGS`.
2. Wait for the client's request `HEADERS` and capture its odd stream ID.
3. Send a flood of `PUSH_PROMISE` frames (`flags = END_HEADERS`) associated with the captured stream, each promising a fresh even stream ID and carrying a minimal HPACK-encoded header block.
4. Never send the matching response `HEADERS` for any of the promised IDs.
5. The client's `conn.streams` map grows by one entry per `PUSH_PROMISE` frame (~148 bytes/entry); memory grows linearly and the BEAM process eventually crashes with OOM.

### Impact

Remote, unauthenticated denial-of-service against any process using Mint as an HTTP/2 client against an untrusted or attacker-influenced server. Server push is on by default, so no application code change can prevent it short of disabling push or upgrading. Affected populations include outbound HTTP/2 clients in web backends, webhook delivery systems, scrapers, federated and proxy components, and any service that follows redirects to third-party HTTP/2 origins.

## Workarounds

Disable HTTP/2 server push on connections to untrusted servers by passing `client_settings: [enable_push: false]` to `'Elixir.Mint.HTTP':connect/4`. Mint will then reject any inbound `PUSH_PROMISE` frame with a `PROTOCOL_ERROR` before the vulnerable code path is reached.

## References

* Introduction commit: https://github.com/elixir-mint/mint/commit/65c6394d05a1b8aa4a7461708c3aa173e8d7a5cf
* Patch commit: https://github.com/elixir-mint/mint/commit/70b97b6a5209fb288b0e04d8e657dda26c59de67

summary: Content-Length header accepts non-RFC "+" sign prefix
description:
### Summary

Mint's HTTP/1 client accepts `Content-Length` header values with a leading `+` sign (e.g. `+0`, `+123`), which RFC 7230 forbids (`Content-Length = 1*DIGIT`). On a connection shared with a strict fronting proxy or load balancer, this parser disagreement is a response-smuggling primitive: the proxy frames the body one way, Mint frames it another, and bytes meant for one response leak into the next consumer's response stream.

### Details

`'Elixir.Mint.HTTP1.Parse':content_length_header/1` in `lib/mint/http1/parse.ex` parses the header value with `Integer.parse/1`. By design, `Integer.parse/1` accepts an optional `+` or `-` sign prefix. The `length >= 0` guard rules out negatives, but inputs such as `"+0"`, `"+123"`, or `"+1"` pass through and are returned as valid lengths.

A strict proxy or load balancer rejects or reframes `Content-Length: +0\r\n`, while Mint silently treats it as `0`. When Mint reuses the socket (keep-alive, pipelining, or any pooled connection) and the connection is shared with a proxy that frames the same bytes differently, trailing bytes the proxy attributes to response N are attributed by Mint to response N+1. Across trust boundaries (shared pools, multi-tenant fronting) this enables response smuggling.

### PoC

1. Stand up a raw TCP server that returns `HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: +0\r\nConnection: keep-alive\r\n\r\n<smuggled bytes>`.
2. Connect a Mint HTTP/1 client to the server and issue a request.
3. Observe that Mint reports the response as status 200 with `Content-Length: "+0"` and an empty body, leaving the smuggled bytes sitting in the socket buffer for the next response.

### Impact

Response-smuggling / request-response desync primitive in Mint's HTTP/1 client parser. Anyone using Mint (directly or via Finch, Tesla's Mint adapter, Req, etc.) to talk through a shared or pooled connection where a fronting proxy enforces RFC 7230 strictly while Mint does not is exposed. The attacker is the response producer (a malicious or compromised upstream, or anything that can inject bytes into a shared origin response); exploitation into a cross-request data leak additionally requires the deployment to share a Mint connection across trust boundaries.

## References

* Introduction commit: https://github.com/elixir-mint/mint/commit/65e0e86d799a6d3b08e4372fccdd9747535e0dd6
* Patch commit: https://github.com/elixir-mint/mint/commit/47e48027480228e4e32a0b4df39db497b4804921

cwes.name: Inconsistent Interpretation of HTTP Requests ('HTTP Request/Response Smuggling')

description:
### Summary

Mint's HTTP/2 client accumulates `CONTINUATION` header-block fragments into a per-connection buffer with no cap on size or frame count. A malicious or compromised HTTP/2 server can drive the client's memory to arbitrary size by streaming an endless chain of `CONTINUATION` frames after a `HEADERS` frame that omits `END_HEADERS`, causing memory exhaustion and BEAM process death. A single connection to an attacker-controlled HTTP/2 endpoint is sufficient.

### Details

When Mint's HTTP/2 receive path observes a `HEADERS` frame without the `END_HEADERS` flag, `'Elixir.Mint.HTTP2':handle_headers/3` parks the unparsed header-block fragment in `conn.headers_being_processed`. Every subsequent `CONTINUATION` frame on that stream is then appended to the accumulator by `'Elixir.Mint.HTTP2':handle_continuation/3`.

Nothing in the receive path bounds this accumulator: there is no per-stream size cap, no `CONTINUATION` frame-count cap, and `max_header_list_size` is only enforced on outgoing requests (its default is `:infinity`, and the only enforcement helper inspects `server_settings` for request encoding, never inbound header blocks). Each `CONTINUATION` payload can be up to the peer-advertised `SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE`, so the attacker can grow `headers_being_processed` to arbitrary size at line rate.

### PoC

1. Stand up a raw TCP server that speaks the HTTP/2 handshake.
2. After the client's request `HEADERS` arrives, respond with a `HEADERS` frame on stream 1 with `flags = 0` (no `END_HEADERS`, no `END_STREAM`) and an empty header-block fragment.
3. Stream `CONTINUATION` frames on stream 1, each with `flags = 0` and a payload up to `SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE`. Never set `END_HEADERS`.
4. The client's process memory grows linearly with the flood and the BEAM process eventually crashes with OOM.

### Impact

Remote, unauthenticated denial-of-service against any process using Mint as an HTTP/2 client against an untrusted or attacker-influenced server. A single connection is sufficient to drive memory to arbitrary size and crash the BEAM process. The default Mint configuration is vulnerable; no client-side opt-in is required. Scored CVSS v4.0 8.2 (HIGH).

## Workarounds

Restrict Mint to HTTP/1 on connections to untrusted servers by passing `protocols: [:http1]` to `'Elixir.Mint.HTTP':connect/4`. This avoids the vulnerable HTTP/2 receive path entirely, at the cost of losing HTTP/2 for those connections.

## References

* Introduction commit: https://github.com/elixir-mint/mint/commit/596ca4304504be68939c4929e0831557097962b8
* Patch commit: https://github.com/elixir-mint/mint/commit/b662d127d3028b5426c88d4c9cc7fe430491a10b

summary: CRLF injection in HTTP request line via unvalidated `method`/`target`
description:
### Summary

Mint's HTTP/1 request encoder splices the caller-supplied `method` and `target` directly into the request line without character validation. An application that forwards attacker-controlled input as the HTTP method or the target to `Mint.HTTP.request/5` is exposed to request-line CRLF injection, allowing the attacker to terminate the request line early, inject arbitrary headers, and pipeline a fully attacker-chosen second request onto the same TCP connection.

### Details

`encode_request_line/2` in `lib/mint/http1/request.ex` writes `method` and `target` to the wire verbatim. `encode_headers/1` validates header names and values, but there is no equivalent `validate_method!/1`.

Mint 1.7.0 added `validate_request_target/2`, which rejects CRLF and other control characters in `target` by default and closes the path/query vector. The `method` field remains unvalidated, so a CRLF-bearing method such as `"GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nX-Smuggled: 1\r\nGET /admin"` is accepted and written to the socket as-is. Bytes after the first `\r\n` are interpreted by the peer as an injected header, or, with a second `\r\n`, as an additional pipelined request.

### PoC

1. Stand up a Mint-using gateway/proxy that calls `Mint.HTTP.request(conn, method, "/", [], nil)` with `method` taken from caller input.
2. Send a request whose forwarded method is `"GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nX-Smuggled-Header: pwned\r\nGET /admin/delete-everything"`.
3. Observe the bytes received by the upstream server: the smuggled header line and the second request line appear verbatim in the outbound stream.

### Impact

CRLF injection / HTTP request smuggling in the HTTP/1 client encoder, exploitable under default configuration whenever an application passes caller-influenced input as the HTTP method. An attacker who controls the method can inject arbitrary outbound headers (forged `Host`, `Authorization`, cache-poisoning headers) and smuggle additional, fully attacker-chosen requests to the upstream server over the same connection, potentially reaching endpoints the legitimate caller never intended to invoke.

## References

* Introduction commit: https://github.com/elixir-mint/mint/commit/8db1acff30b6a9433762c18b1e1f891b8c1f74f7
* Patch commit: https://github.com/elixir-mint/mint/commit/fad091454cbb7449b19edb8e1fee12ca7cf28c3a

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of CRLF Sequences ('CRLF Injection')
